docs.title: Welcome to RKD as ROCKETDOO!
docs.text:
Version 3.15 of ROCKETDOO — Odoo's performance settings configurable per environment, on top of seeding a VPS instance with your development database, a pre-flight that stops a deploy before it breaks, Enterprise and third-party repos that reach the server, HTTPS on the VPS, and Odoo 20.

Rocketdoo is a development and delivery platform for Odoo teams that standardizes, automates, and abstracts the lifecycle of Odoo environments, from local development all the way to deployment.

Rocketdoo is a Python-based framework designed to provide a fast and efficient development environment.

With Rocketdoo, you can deploy one or several environments for Odoo development in just a few simple steps. It allows you to create new modules or features for both the Enterprise and Community editions.

docs.title: ⚙️ Odoo's performance settings, per environment
docs.text:
New in 3.15. Workers, cron threads, memory and time limits are no longer fixed by the environment's name: a resources block in .rkd/instance.yaml sets them per environment, and rkd instance init asks for them.

environments:
  prod:
    resources:
      limit_time_cpu: 600     # seconds; Odoo's default of 60 halves a large import
      limit_time_real: 1200
      workers: 4

Every field is optional and an absent one keeps the default the environment name implies, so an instance.yaml without the block deploys exactly as it used to.

The case it exists for: a project whose odoo.conf raises the time limits for large imports and heavy reports. Deploying it wrote 60/120 over those values, cutting both operations in half — and editing the file on the server was no fix, because the next deploy rewrites it with no guard, so a hand-tuned value was silently lost.

The memory pre-flight check now adds up this environment's effective values instead of Rocketdoo's own constants, so a figure that does not fit the VPS blocks the deploy before anything is written, and names it. Sizing is still never read from the server: physical RAM is not available RAM.

The seven values, the defaults per environment, and what native deploys inherit

docs.title: What's New in 3.14
docs.text: Nine releases separate 3.5 from 3.14.3, and almost none of them added a command. What they did was turn rkd instance from a deploy you had to supervise into one that checks the server before it touches it — plus Odoo 20, a pack that leaves your secrets at home, and a GUI that stops freezing.

docs.title: 🌱 Seed a VPS instance with your development database
docs.text:
New in 3.14. A deployed environment no longer has to start from an empty database. Pick a local database when you configure the environment and the deploy dumps it, transfers it, restores it on the server — filestore included — and neutralizes what must not run there.

rkd instance init             # "Database for stage:" → pick a local database, or none
rkd instance deploy -e stage

Three rules are worth knowing before you use it:

  • It happens once per environment. The deploy writes a mark inside the restored database, so a redeploy never restores again. Seeding a second time means dropping the database on the VPS by hand — deliberately, because the alternative is a flag that overwrites a client's production with a development dump.
  • An existing database is never overwritten. If the target already serves an Odoo that Rocketdoo did not seed, the deploy refuses and says so.
  • Neutralization depends on the target. Both regenerate the database UUID and disable the Mailpit mail server, which points at a host that does not exist on the VPS. Only staging also disables scheduled actions, mail servers and payment providers — doing that to production would stop the crons of the very instance you are launching.

The admin password of a seeded database is not replaced: its users keep theirs.

How to configure it, and what the pre-flight checks

docs.title: 🛡️ A pre-flight that stops before it breaks, and a dry run that writes nothing
docs.text:
Since 3.11. Both deployers now open with a pre-flight: a single read-only SSH session that collects facts about the server and sorts them into blockers and warnings. A blocker stops the deploy before anything is written.

--dry-run used to print "Deployment successful" without touching the VPS — and still wrote a secrets file locally. Now it runs that same pre-flight, connects only to read, writes nothing, and exits non-zero when something blocks. So this finally means what it looks like:

rkd instance deploy -e prod --dry-run && rkd instance deploy -e prod

It checks the connection, Docker, sudo, the remote path, disk space, memory, your SSH key and agent, the Gitman file and its repositories, the Enterprise directory, the PostgreSQL version, the database identifiers, Traefik and the public URL.

docs.title: 🏢 Enterprise and third-party repos finally reach the server
docs.text:
Since 3.11, completed in 3.13. Choosing Enterprise in the wizard used to declare the directory everywhere and put it nowhere: Odoo started without the addons. Gitman repos were cloned on the VPS and never entered the addons_path.

Enterprise now travels either way — rsync sends your local enterprise/, or clone fetches odoo/enterprise on the server through a forwarded SSH agent, leaving no credentials behind. Since 3.13 the native path installs Gitman repos exactly where the Docker path does and builds the same canonical order: enterprise, extra-addons, nested dirs, gitman.

Docker or native is a choice about packaging, not about what you get.

docs.title: 🌐 HTTPS on the VPS: rkd instance traefik
docs.text:
New in 3.12. The Odoo container only exposes its port; something has to answer on 80/443 and get the certificate.

rkd instance traefik -e prod

Installs Traefik on that environment's server, once per host, with the same configuration rkd traefik renders locally. It is safe to run again — files you tuned and certificates already issued are kept — and the deploy never runs it for you, because ports 80 and 443 belong to the host and not to one project.

docs.title: 🐘 Odoo 20
docs.text:
Since 3.7. odoo20-ce and odoo20-ee join the golden paths, and odoo20-ce is built by CI on every release.

The image needs no Dockerfile change, but PostgreSQL does: Odoo 20 requires 16 or newer, against 13 for Odoo 19 and 12 all the way back to 15. A project on PostgreSQL 14 cannot move to Odoo 20 without migrating the database first, and the matrix now refuses that pairing instead of letting it through.

Create it from the terminal. The GUI's Setup form still stops at Odoo 19, so use rkd init --profile odoo20-ce and then manage the project from the GUI as usual.

The full compatibility matrix

docs.title: 🔐 A pack that leaves your secrets at home
docs.text:
Since 3.9.2. rkd pack used to put the sender's own credentials in the ZIP it handed to someone else.

The archive no longer carries .ssh/, .rkd/secrets/, .rkd/instance.yaml, .rkd/deploy.yaml, traefik/certs/acme.json or any *.env, and no symlink enters it — a link pointing at a secrets file used to exfiltrate it. The panel names everything it left out, which is exactly the list the receiver has to rewrite. Since 3.10 the verifier also reads the first 64 KiB of each entry looking for PEM headers, rather than trusting filenames. Two credentials still travel on purpose — odoo_pg_pass and config/odoo.conf — because the shared environment does not start without them.

docs.title: 🪪 A restored copy gets its own Compose identity
docs.text:
Since 3.9. Two copies sharing one Compose project name meant Compose treated the original's containers as its own — and the copy's restore ran DROP DATABASE on the original's data.

rkd unpack now detects the clash, through docker compose ls and volume labels (a project brought down without -v is absent from the first but its volumes are still there), and rewrites the whole identity of the copy: project name, image, every container name, volumes and db_host. It is all-or-nothing, and if Docker does not answer nothing is renamed — it never guesses.

docs.title: 📧 Mailpit picks a free port
docs.text:
Since 3.9.1. Two Rocketdoo projects with rkd mail on no longer collide.

mail on keeps the ports declared in the compose file when they are free and takes the next free one when they are not, counting ports declared by a sibling project that is switched off. It prints which one it took and writes it back, so a browser bookmark keeps working. The internal 1025 never changes: Odoo always talks to mailpit:1025.

docs.title: ⚡ A GUI that stops freezing
docs.text:
Since 3.14.3. Thirty-five GUI handlers were declared async without a single await, so FastAPI ran them on the event loop and any blocking work froze the whole interface — log WebSockets included. A Docker build could hold it for five minutes.

They now run in the thread pool. Two more things the GUI gained along the way: it no longer needs internet to draw itself (Vue is vendored, so a blocked CDN used to leave a blank page), and the token screen has a field to paste into, for when you reach http://localhost:8070 without the query string.

docs.title: 🖥️ A GUI that says where you are, in your language
docs.text:
The interface was rebuilt around what changes while you work:

  • A permanent top bar with the active project and a pill counting running containers, so no screen leaves you guessing which project you are acting on.
  • Grouped sidebar navigation — Project, Environment, Publish — plus a new Projects screen that discovers every Rocketdoo project on the host and switches between them without restarting the server.
  • A light theme that meets WCAG AA contrast, and with no saved choice the GUI follows your operating system instead of always starting dark.
  • Spanish and English, switchable from the top bar. What the GUI only relays — Docker logs, addon names, container names, raw docker compose ps status — is left untouched in both.

The ten screens, with screenshots

docs.title: ⚙️ CI for your project (rkd ci)
docs.text:
rkd ci init writes a GitHub Actions workflow into your project that lints your addons and installs them against a real Odoo:

rkd ci init        # writes .github/workflows/rkd-ci.yml
rkd ci prepare     # regenerates what a clean clone does not carry
rkd ci modules     # the installable modules Odoo can reach

It never overwrites a workflow that differs from what it would write, and the expensive install job is limited to pull requests by default, because Actions minutes are a shared quota on private repos.

What the generated workflow does, and what is outside it

docs.title: 📁 Nested addons Odoo can actually reach
docs.text: Odoo reads a static addons_path, so a module at addons/oca/web_responsive was invisible unless that subdirectory was listed. rkd up, rkd restart, rkd build --rebuild, rkd ci prepare, the GUI's Up and the per-module update now keep the path in sync with what is actually under addons/; rkd info warns without writing. Entries that are not Rocketdoo's own — Odoo's default, enterprise, Gitman's external_addons, your own paths — are kept exactly as they are, in order.

docs.title: 📧 rkd mail configures the mail server, not just the transport
docs.text:
Since 3.3. rkd mail on now also creates the ir.mail_server record Mailpit (rkd) in your database, so Odoo actually routes through Mailpit. off only archives it — it never deletes, so a mail server of your own is never at risk. Projects with more than one database need --db NAME.

The record, the --db flag and a known limit

docs.title: 🔑 The GUI asks for a session token
docs.text:
Since 3.4, every rkd gui prints a URL carrying a session token, and the API rejects anything without it. The token is good for as long as that server runs, and restarting it issues a new one. Browsing to http://localhost:8070 on its own no longer works — use the URL it prints, or --open.

Why, and what it does not protect against

docs.title: What's New in 3.2
docs.text: Version 3.2 does not add a new subsystem: it makes the existing ones predictable.

docs.title: 🧭 Golden Paths (rkd profiles)
docs.text:
A golden path is a named, supported combination of Odoo version, edition and PostgreSQL version. Rocketdoo shipped ten of them at the time — Odoo 15 to 19, Community and Enterprise; today there are twelve — and they became the source of truth for both the wizard and non-interactive setup:

rkd profiles list              # the whole matrix
rkd profiles show odoo18-ce    # detail of one profile
rkd init --profile odoo18-ce   # create the environment without any prompts

Three of them (odoo15-ce, odoo18-ce, odoo19-ee) were built by CI on every release PR; the rest are best effort. Odoo↔PostgreSQL compatibility is validated now, so the wizard can no longer produce an unsupported pairing — Odoo 19, for instance, requires PostgreSQL 13 or above.

The full matrix and support levels

docs.title: ✅ Test suite and a real CI gate
docs.text:
Rocketdoo now has a pytest suite of over 900 tests, plus ruff for linting, running on every pull request across Python 3.10 to 3.13, with Docker end-to-end tests, a package build check and a render-and-build pass over the golden paths. Nothing is continue-on-error any more: a red job means the change does not merge.

How to run it before opening a PR

docs.title: 🔧 Fixes worth upgrading for
docs.text:
• Docker build failed on Odoo 18 and 19. The generated Dockerfile removed the PEP 668 marker in its own layer, but apt install python3-dev pulls in the python3.N package, which puts the file back — so the later pip install died with externally-managed-environment. Only Ubuntu noble images (odoo:18.0, odoo:19.0) ship that marker, which is why the older versions were unaffected. All five images are now built in CI.
  • rkd pack always failed with UnboundLocalError when run with --no-db, or before any database existed — the two normal ways to use it. Present in 3.1.8 and earlier.
  • The GUI API accepted requests from any origin. rkd gui now only accepts calls from its own origin. Binding to 127.0.0.1 was never protection here: the request comes from the user's own browser, so any page visited while the GUI was running could list the filesystem and stop containers.

docs.title: What's New in ROCKETDOO Version 3
docs.text: Version 3 is the most complete release of ROCKETDOO to date. It keeps everything from version 2 and adds four major new capabilities:

docs.title: 🖥️ Graphical User Interface (GUI)
docs.text:
Rocketdoo v3 ships with its own web-based GUI, launched directly from the terminal with a single command:

rkd gui

The GUI opens in your browser at the URL rkd gui prints — since 3.4 that URL carries a session token — and provides:

  • Dashboard — project overview with container status, Odoo version, PostgreSQL version, and quick access links.
  • Container controls — start, stop, restart, build, pull, and remove containers without typing Docker commands.
  • Live log viewer — real-time streaming logs from any container.
  • Mail (Mailpit) — enable/disable the email testing service directly from the interface.
  • Modules — list and manage Odoo add-on modules.
  • Deploy — run deployment operations from the GUI.
  • Instance — manage VPS deployment targets.
  • Pack / Unpack — share or restore full development environments.
  • Gitman — manage third-party repository dependencies.
  • Traefik — configure the reverse proxy integration.
  • Dark and light mode — toggle the theme to match your preference.

Learn more about the GUI

docs.title: 📧 Mailpit Email Testing (rkd mail)
docs.text:
The new mail command integrates Mailpit — a local SMTP server and web UI that captures all outgoing emails from Odoo instead of sending them.

rkd mail on       # Enable Mailpit and configure Odoo SMTP
rkd mail off      # Disable Mailpit and restore defaults
rkd mail status   # Show current status
rkd mail open     # Open the Mailpit web UI in the browser

docs.title: 🌐 Traefik Reverse Proxy (rkd traefik)
docs.text:
The traefik command makes it easy to expose your local Odoo instance using a custom domain, either for local development or full production with HTTPS and Let's Encrypt.

rkd traefik on      # Interactive setup: domain, mode (local/production)
rkd traefik off     # Remove Traefik integration from the project
rkd traefik status  # Show current Traefik configuration
rkd traefik guide   # Step-by-step guide for local domain setup

docs.title: 🚀 Full VPS Instance Deployment (rkd instance)
docs.text:
The instance command allows you to deploy a complete Odoo instance to a VPS — either as a Dockerized build or as a native installation — using a simple interactive wizard.

rkd instance init                # Configure stage/prod environments interactively
rkd instance deploy --env stage  # Deploy to staging
rkd instance deploy --env prod   # Deploy to production
rkd instance status              # Show configured deployment targets

docs.title: From Version 2 — Still Available
docs.text:
All features from ROCKETDOO v2 are fully preserved:

  • rkd scaffold / rkd init — project scaffolding and configuration wizard.
  • rkd up, rkd down, rkd restart, rkd stop, rkd build, rkd status, rkd logs — Docker container management.
  • rkd pack / rkd unpack — share and restore full environments.
  • rkd del -i — clean up .Identifier files created by WSL2.
  • rkd deploy — module deployment to Odoo SH, VPS, or Dockerized instances.

On the following page, you can find detailed information about deployments using rkd. >>> Deployment

Rocketdoo v3 is more powerful and easier to use than ever before...

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This tool was designed for developers who are just getting started with Odoo, as well as for experienced developers who want to quickly deploy environments and focus solely on building new modules and features.

It’s important to note that Rocketdoo is just one of many tools available in the Odoo development ecosystem. It does not aim to be the only or the best option — rather, it’s a practical solution that adds value, covers common development needs, and optimizes and automates the developer’s workflow.

We know that the Odoo ERP system is broad, powerful, and complex. Depending on the client, the business requirements, or the localization being implemented, it’s necessary to consider a series of dependencies that go beyond pure development. These may include required Python libraries, specific dependencies for certain features, third-party modules, or external repositories needed to ensure a successful implementation.

All these requirements and configurations often become a real burden for developers.

That’s why Rocketdoo was created — to provide an automated and intuitive environment that serves both individual developers and development teams. Rocketdoo simplifies the process of setting up a development environment and lets you focus on what really matters: building new modules and features.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
To better understand what Rocketdoo is and how to use it properly, let’s go through a brief description of the required tools and their purpose.

First, it’s important to mention that Rocketdoo was designed and developed to create development environments on Linux-based operating systems, such as Ubuntu or Debian. We consider Linux to be the most suitable system for working with this framework for the following reasons.

Rocketdoo relies on the following tools to perform its functions:

  • Docker y Docker Compose.
  • Git y GitHub (or any version control manager).
  • Llave SSH for managing private repositories.
  • Gitman.
  • Python and its packages manager pip or pipx.
  • Command Line Interface (CLI) usage.
  • Visual Studio Code.
  • Required Visual Studio Code extensions (listed later)

This list of required tools — especially Docker and Docker Compose — is one of the main reasons why we recommend using Rocketdoo on a Linux operating system.

However, we understand that many developers prefer using Windows. In that case, we strongly recommend using the Windows Subsystem for Linux version 2: WSL2.

docs.title: 🚀 Contribution Guide for Rocketdoo
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to Rocketdoo! This guide describes the complete path a change travels: from spotting a bug or proposing an improvement, to seeing that change published on PyPI.

The official repository is HDM-soft/rocketdoo.

docs.title: Table of contents
docs.text:
• Golden rules
  • Branching model
  • The path of a contribution
  • Step 1 — Open the issue
  • Step 2 — Set up the development environment
  • Step 3 — Create the working branch
  • Step 4 — Develop and commit
  • Step 5 — Test before opening the PR
  • Step 6 — Open the Pull Request against dev/v3
  • Step 7 — Review and merge
  • Step 8 — Promotion to production
  • Versioning and releases
  • Urgent hotfix
  • Code conventions
  • Common problems

docs.title: Golden rules
docs.text:
Before writing a single line of code, five rules that shape the whole process:

  1. Every task starts with an issue. No issue, no branch. The issue number names the branch and appears in the commits and in the PR.
  2. Never work directly on main, test/v3 or dev/v3. Always a short-lived branch created from dev/v3.
  3. No contribution PR targets main. Changes enter through dev/v3, and maintainers promote them to test/v3 and then to main.
  4. Contributors don't touch the version. The pyproject.toml bump is done by the maintainer cutting the release, in a dedicated commit. See Versioning and releases.
  5. One PR = one self-contained change. If you're solving two distinct problems, that's two issues and two branches.

docs.title: Branching model
docs.text:
main              ← stable version · merging a PR here publishes to PyPI (CI)
  ↑ release PR (opened by a maintainer)
test/v3           ← QA gate: the package is installed from this branch and smoke-tested
  ↑ tested-integration PR (opened by a maintainer)
dev/v3            ← development integration · base of every working branch
  ↑ your contribution PR
fix/123-slug · feat/124-slug · mig/125-slug · chore/126-slug

Promotion path of any change:

<type>/N-slug  →  dev/v3  →  test/v3  →  main  →  PyPI

test/v3 is the intermediate branch between development and production. It exists to test the installed package (not the local repo): a change that works in your clone can still fail once it's built and installed with pipx. That filter is what keeps a broken version from reaching PyPI.

dev/v2 is the previous, already stabilized line; it only receives occasional back-ports.

docs.title: The path of a contribution
docs.text:
This is the full journey, end to end:

issue #123  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │  describes the problem: repro steps, expected vs. actual, environment
  │
  ├─ branch  fix/123-short-description       created from dev/v3
  │          commits "FIX: ..." with "Refs #123" in the body
  │          local test: pipx install + rkd scaffold in an empty folder
  │
  ├─ PR → dev/v3        "Refs #123"   → maintainer review → merge
  │
  ├─ PR → test/v3       QA gate: installed from the branch, checklist run
  │
  └─ PR → main          "Closes #123" → CI builds and publishes to PyPI
                        → tag vX.Y.Z + GitHub Release → the issue is closed

The first three blocks are your responsibility as a contributor. The last two are executed by maintainers, but it helps to know them to understand why certain things are asked for in the PR.

docs.title: Step 1 — Open the issue
docs.text: The issue is the starting point: it provides context, lets the approach be discussed before you invest time in code, and gives the branch its name.

docs.title: 1.1 Search for duplicates
docs.text:
# With GitHub CLI
gh issue list --repo HDM-soft/rocketdoo --search "unpack filestore" --state all -L 10

Or from the web: repository issues.

docs.title: 1.2 Reproduce the problem in a clean environment
docs.text:
Rocketdoo generates the whole project structure with rkd scaffold, so the reproduction must happen in an empty folder, using the published version:

mkdir -p /tmp/rkd-repro && cd /tmp/rkd-repro
rkd --version        # write down the exact version
rkd scaffold
rkd init
# ... the command that fails

Write down: the exact command, the full output (or traceback), the Rocketdoo version, your operating system, and your Python and Docker versions.

docs.title: 1.3 Create the issue
docs.text:
gh issue create --repo HDM-soft/rocketdoo \
  --title "FIX: rkd unpack does not restore the filestore when the volume is slow to mount" \
  --label bug \
  --body-file /tmp/issue.md

Or from the web with the New issue button.

Title: a single line, using the same prefix the final commit will carry (FIX:, FEAT:, MIG:, DOC:, REF:), describing the symptom for a bug or the expected outcome for an improvement.

Suggested labels: bug, enhancement, migration, docs, ci, v3, priority:high.

docs.title: 1.4 Template — bug report
docs.text:
## Description
<what fails, in one or two sentences>

## Steps to reproduce
1. `mkdir /tmp/rkd-test && cd /tmp/rkd-test`
2. `rkd scaffold`
3. `rkd init` (values used: Odoo 17.0, Community, no gitman, ports 8069/8888)
4. `rkd unpack`

## Expected behavior
<what should happen>

## Actual behavior
<what happens; paste the traceback or relevant output in a code block>

## Environment
- rocketdoo: `rkd --version` → 3.15.0
- Python: 3.12.3
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2)
- Docker: 27.x / Compose v2.x

## Impact
<blocking | degraded | cosmetic>

docs.title: 1.5 Template — improvement or feature
docs.text:
## Current problem or limitation
<what can't be done today, and who it affects>

## Proposal
<proposed behavior; if it adds a command or option, show the interface>

## Alternatives considered
<discarded options and why>

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] <verifiable condition 1>
- [ ] <verifiable condition 2>
- [ ] Documented in the README and in the documentation

## Versioning impact
<patch | minor | major> — <justification>

Keep the issue number. It's the N you'll use in the branch, the commits and the PR.

docs.title: Step 2 — Set up the development environment
Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or higher (matching requires-python in pyproject.toml)
  • Git
  • Up-to-date pip (pip install --upgrade pip)
  • pipx (recommended for testing the CLI)
  • GitHub CLI (gh) — optional, but it simplifies issues and PRs

docs.title: 1. Fork the repository
docs.text: On GitHub, click Fork in the top-right corner of HDM-soft/rocketdoo.

docs.title: 2. Clone your fork locally
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/rocketdoo.git
cd rocketdoo

docs.title: 3. Add the original repository as a remote
docs.text:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git

This lets you sync with changes from the original repo whenever needed:

git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/dev/v3

docs.title: 4. Development virtual environment
docs.text:
To modify the code and see the changes reflected immediately, use a dedicated virtual environment:

# From the root of the cloned repo
python -m venv venv-dev

# Linux / macOS
source venv-dev/bin/activate
# Windows
.\venv-dev\Scripts\activate

docs.title: 5. Install the package and the development dependencies
docs.text:
Install Rocketdoo in editable mode together with the tooling CI uses — pytest, pytest-cov, ruff and httpx:

pip install -e . -r requirements-dev.txt

Editable mode means your changes to the source take effect without reinstalling. Check that the suite is green before you touch anything, so you know any later failure is yours:

pytest

docs.title: Step 3 — Create the working branch
docs.text:
Always from an up-to-date dev/v3, never from main:

git fetch upstream
git checkout dev/v3
git pull --ff-only upstream dev/v3

Naming: <type>/<issue-number>-<short-slug>

git checkout -b fix/123-unpack-filestore
# Examples:
# git checkout -b feat/124-multi-model-support
# git checkout -b mig/125-odoo-18
# git checkout -b chore/126-update-dependencies

If you use GitHub CLI, this command creates the branch already linked to the issue on GitHub:

gh issue develop 123 --base dev/v3 --name fix/123-unpack-filestore --checkout

docs.title: Branch types
docs.text: Type When to use it Base fix/ Bug fix dev/v3 feat/ New feature or command dev/v3 mig/ Migration (Odoo version, dependency, config format) dev/v3 chore/ Maintenance (deps, CI, cleanup) dev/v3 docs/ Documentation only dev/v3 refactor/ Refactoring without behavior change dev/v3 hotfix/ Emergency with production broken main

docs.title: Step 4 — Develop and commit
docs.text:
One commit per logical change, with uppercase prefixes (the ones used by the project history):

Prefix When to use it FIX: Bug fix FEAT: New feature or command UPD: General update (CI, config, docs bundled with code) UPG: Version bump only (UPG: version 3.2.0) — reserved for maintainers REF: Refactoring without behavior change DOC: Documentation TEST: Adding or fixing tests DEL: Removing code or artifacts

The issue is referenced in the commit body:

git commit -m "FIX: wait for the volume mount before restoring the filestore

Refs #123"

Use Refs #123 in intermediate commits. Closes #123 is reserved for the release PR into main, because GitHub only auto-closes issues when a PR is merged into the default branch.

docs.title: Step 5 — Test before opening the PR
5.1 Install your local code and run the minimum cycle
docs.text:
pipx install /path/to/your/rocketdoo/clone --force

mkdir -p /tmp/rkd-test && cd /tmp/rkd-test
rkd scaffold
rkd init
# ... and the command your change touches

docs.title: 5.2 Pre-flight of the CI gate
docs.text:
Continuous integration runs on every pull request and nothing is continue-on-error: a red job means the change does not merge. The single required status check is ci-ok, which aggregates all the others:

Job What it runs Lint (ruff) ruff check . and ruff format --check . Tests (py3.10 … py3.13) the whole pytest suite, with coverage, on the four supported Python versions E2E with Docker the tests marked docker — on CI they must not silently skip Build distributions python -m build, twine check, and proof that the wheel really ships templates/ and the GUI Golden path … rkd scaffold && rkd init --profile … for odoo15-ce, odoo18-ce and odoo19-ee, then docker compose config over the result Docker build (odoo:…) a real docker build against the five supported Odoo images — only on PRs to test/v3 or main

Run the same thing locally before pushing:

source venv-dev/bin/activate
pip install -e . -r requirements-dev.txt

ruff check .
ruff format --check .
pytest                      # the whole suite
pytest -m "not docker"      # if there is no Docker daemon available

Tests marked docker skip themselves when no daemon is running locally, but they do run on CI, so a change that only works on your machine will still be caught.

If your change touches a Jinja template, the snapshot tests fail on purpose. Read the diff first; if the new render is the intended one, regenerate the reference and commit it:

UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 pytest tests/test_templates.py

If any of this reports errors, the PR will go red.

docs.title: 5.3 Test a branch without touching your production install
docs.text: To review someone else's branch (or your own, already pushed) without uninstalling your working Rocketdoo:

docs.title: Option A — With pipx (recommended for the CLI) ✅
docs.text:
pipx installs into an isolated environment and exposes the commands globally. With --suffix, the production version and the test version coexist:

pipx install "git+https://github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git@fix/123-unpack-filestore" --suffix=-test

That gives you two commands in parallel:

rkd             # ← production version installed from PyPI (untouched)
rkd-test        # ← version from the test branch

The suffix applies to every command the package exposes, so rocketdoo and rocketdoo-test are available too. For pipx, the installed package is named rocketdoo-test.

To update after new commits are pushed to the branch, and to clean up when you're done:

pipx reinstall rocketdoo-test
pipx uninstall rocketdoo-test

docs.title: Option B — With pip inside a venv (for imports or scripts)
docs.text:
mkdir test-rocketdoo && cd test-rocketdoo
python -m venv venv-test
source venv-test/bin/activate   # Linux / macOS
# .\venv-test\Scripts\activate  # Windows

pip install "git+https://github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git@fix/123-unpack-filestore"

# update after new commits
pip install --force-reinstall "git+https://github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git@fix/123-unpack-filestore"

docs.title: Private repo: authentication with a token
docs.text:
pip install "git+https://YOUR_TOKEN@github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git@fix/123-unpack-filestore"
Method When to use it pipx install git+... --suffix=-test Recommended. Test CLI commands without touching the production install pipx install /local/path --force Test your own code before pushing pip install git+... inside a venv Test Python imports or script integrations

docs.title: Step 6 — Open the Pull Request against dev/v3
docs.text:
git push -u origin fix/123-unpack-filestore

gh pr create --repo HDM-soft/rocketdoo \
  --base dev/v3 --head YOUR_USERNAME:fix/123-unpack-filestore \
  --title "FIX: wait for the volume mount before restoring the filestore" \
  --body-file /tmp/pr.md

Or from the web with the Compare & pull request button, making sure the target is dev/v3.

The PR targets dev/v3, never main or test/v3. A PR against main triggers the PyPI publishing workflow and will be closed without merging.

docs.title: PR template
docs.text:
## What changes
<summary in 2-4 lines>

Refs #123

## Why
<root cause of the bug, or need for the improvement>

## How to test it
```bash
pipx install "git+https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/rocketdoo.git@fix/123-unpack-filestore" --suffix=-test
mkdir /tmp/rkd-pr && cd /tmp/rkd-pr
rkd-test scaffold && rkd-test init && rkd-test unpack
```

Expected result: <...>

## Verified
- [ ] The reproduction of #123 no longer happens
- [ ] `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` clean
- [ ] `pytest` green
- [ ] The new behavior is covered by at least one test
- [ ] Local pipx cycle OK
- [ ] The version in `pyproject.toml` was not modified
- [ ] No build artifacts were added to the repo

Use Refs #123, not Closes #123: auto-closing only happens on merge to main.

docs.title: Step 7 — Review and merge
docs.text:
Once the PR is open, request a review from the maintainers (the Reviewers field, or by mentioning them in a comment). No PR is merged without at least one approval.

What reviewers look at:

  • The change solves what the issue describes, and nothing more.
  • No version changes in pyproject.toml, README.md or LICENSE.
  • No build artifacts slipped in (dist/, build/, *.egg-info).
  • The ci-ok check is green: ruff clean, the whole pytest suite passing, and a test covering the new behavior.
  • The new behavior is documented if it changes how a command is used.
  • There is a concrete way to reproduce and verify the fix.

If changes are requested: commit onto the same branch and push; the PR updates itself. Don't open a new PR.

git commit -m "FIX: apply review feedback

Refs #123"
git push

Once approved, a maintainer merges it into dev/v3 (squashing if the branch has back-and-forth commits) and deletes the remote branch. From there your change travels along with the rest of the integration.

docs.title: Step 8 — Promotion to production
docs.text: These two PRs are opened by maintainers. They're documented here so it's clear where every change ends up.

docs.title: 8.1 dev/v3 → test/v3 (QA gate)
docs.text:
Before opening this PR, the maintainer applies the version bump on dev/v3. After the merge, the package is tested as installed from the branch, not from the local repo:

pipx install "git+https://github.com/HDM-soft/rocketdoo.git@test/v3" --suffix=-test
rocketdoo-test --version

QA checklist: scaffold, init, info, up/status/logs/down, mail on|off|status (with --db on a multi-database project), traefik on|off|status, deploy init|list-modules, ci init|prepare|modules, gui (opened on the tokenised URL it prints), pack/unpack if the change touches them, and the reproduction of every included issue, verifying it no longer happens.

If something fails at this point, it's fixed on a new branch from dev/v3 (back to Step 3), never on test/v3 itself.

docs.title: 8.2 test/v3 → main (release)
docs.text:
This PR does carry Closes #123 (one line per included issue) plus the release notes. Merging it triggers .github/workflows/publish-rkd.yml, which runs the tests, builds the package and publishes it to PyPI via Trusted Publishing.

After publication, and manually: tag the merge commit (git tag -a vX.Y.Z origin/main), create the GitHub Release, close any issues that didn't close themselves, and back-merge main into test/v3 and dev/v3.

docs.title: Versioning and releases
docs.text:
If you're contributing, don't touch the version. The bump is done by the maintainer cutting the release, on dev/v3, in a dedicated UPG: version X.Y.Z commit. This avoids conflicts between concurrent branches and duplicate bumps.

The version lives in three files and they must move together in the same commit:

File Field pyproject.toml version = "X.Y.Z" — the packaging source of truth (what PyPI publishes) README.md the ## Version: block LICENSE the Versión: line of the header (bump Fecha: too)

rocketdoo/__init__.py is never edited: it reads the installed version at runtime through importlib.metadata, and the __version__ = "dev" there is only the fallback for a source checkout.

Semantic versioning:

Change Bump Example Bug fix, internal adjustment, documentation patch 3.2.0 → 3.2.1 New command or option, backwards-compatible feature minor 3.2.1 → 3.3.0 Breaking change (CLI, config format, generated layout) major 3.3.0 → 4.0.0

twine upload is never run by hand against production PyPI: PyPI versions are immutable, and a manual upload makes the CI fail afterwards with 400 File already exists. TestPyPI is used to rehearse a publication.

docs.title: Urgent hotfix
docs.text:
Only for broken production, when waiting for the QA gate isn't viable. The branch is created from main:

git fetch upstream
git checkout -b hotfix/130-slug upstream/main

The PR goes straight to main. Since it skips test/v3, local validation is mandatory: build the package, twine check, install the wheel with pipx, and verify the failure is resolved. After publication, back-merging main into test/v3 and dev/v3 is mandatory so the fix isn't lost.

docs.title: Code conventions
docs.text:
• We follow PEP 8 for Python code style.
  • Use type hints wherever possible.
  • All new code must include basic docstrings.
  • If you add a feature, include at least one test covering it.
  • Avoid introducing new dependencies without prior justification and discussion in the related issue.
  • Don't commit build artifacts (dist/, *.egg-info) or local environment files.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Symptom Cause Solution The PR went red on ci-ok One of the aggregated jobs failed Open ci-ok to see which one, then reproduce it locally with Step 5.2 The PR went red on Lint (ruff) Lint or formatting ruff check --fix . and ruff format . A snapshot test fails after editing a template The rendered output no longer matches the reference Review the diff; if it is the intended render, UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 pytest tests/test_templates.py and commit the snapshot The issue didn't close when the PR was merged The PR merged into dev/v3, not the default branch That's expected: it closes with the release PR to main rkd --version shows dev Package installed without metadata (editable checkout) Reinstall with pipx install ... --force Conflict in pyproject.toml when rebasing Your branch touched the version Discard that change: the bump doesn't belong in working branches rkd scaffold fails in the test directory The folder wasn't empty Rocketdoo generates the structure from scratch; use a new folder gh: command not found GitHub CLI not installed Install it from cli.github.com or run the whole flow from the web

docs.title: Questions?
docs.text:
Open a GitHub Discussion or reach out to the project maintainers. Every contribution, no matter how small, is welcome!

This document is part of the official Rocketdoo documentation.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
Here are the most common commands you can use in RKD ROCKETDOO.

You can use either rocketdoo or the shorter alias rkd — both are equivalent.

TIP: Combine any command with --help to see its flags and options. Example: rkd build --help

docs.title: General
docs.text:
• Display Rocketdoo version:
rkd --version
  • Display help and available commands:
rkd --help

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
• Generate the directory and file structure:
rkd scaffold
  • Launch the initialization wizard:
rkd init
  • Or create the environment straight from a supported profile, with no questions asked:
rkd init --profile odoo18-ce
  • Display detailed information about the current project:
rkd info

Since 3.5, rkd info also warns when a module under addons/ sits in a subdirectory that Odoo's addons_path does not cover. It only warns, never writes. What writes the path: rkd up, rkd restart, rkd build --rebuild, rkd ci prepare, the GUI's Up and the per-module update.

docs.title: Golden Paths (rkd profiles)
docs.text:
New in 3.2, extended in 3.7. A golden path is a named, supported combination of Odoo version, edition and PostgreSQL version. Rocketdoo ships twelve of them — Odoo 15 to 20, Community and Enterprise — and they are the source of truth for both the rkd init wizard and rkd init --profile.

  • List the whole matrix:
rkd profiles list

  • Show the details of a single profile:
rkd profiles show odoo19-ce

  • Create that environment end to end, without the wizard:
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
rkd scaffold
rkd init --profile odoo18-ce
rkd up -d

docs.title: Support levels
docs.text:
Level What it means golden CI renders and builds this combination on every release PR. These are the ones to choose. best effort Within Odoo's stated requirements and offered by the wizard, but not built by CI. Reports are welcome, but there is no guarantee.

The golden combinations today are odoo15-ce, odoo18-ce, odoo19-ee and odoo20-ce: between them they cover the three different base images the odoo: images use, both editions, and the current release.

docs.title: Compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Per-image data was read from the published odoo: images; the PostgreSQL minimums come from Odoo's own installation documentation.

Odoo Base Python pip Minimum PostgreSQL Recommended 15.0 debian-bullseye 3.9 20.3.4 12 14 16.0 debian-bullseye 3.9 20.3.4 12 14 17.0 ubuntu-jammy 3.10 22.0.2 12 15 18.0 ubuntu-noble 3.12 24.0 12 16 19.0 ubuntu-noble 3.12 24.0 13 16 20.0 ubuntu-noble 3.12 24.0 16 17

Odoo 19 raised the PostgreSQL minimum from 12 to 13, and Odoo 20 raised it again to 16 — the biggest jump in the series. Rocketdoo validates the pairing when the profile is loaded: a db_version below the minimum for that Odoo version is an error, not a warning, so the wizard can no longer produce an environment that will not start.

Moving an existing project to Odoo 20. Because the image shares its base with 18 and 19, the generated Dockerfile needs no change — but a project sitting on PostgreSQL 14 or 15 cannot simply switch versions. Migrate the database to 16 or newer first; the matrix now refuses the pairing instead of letting it through and failing at startup.

Odoo 19 and AI: Odoo 19's AI features need the pgvector extension, which ships for PostgreSQL 15 and above. rkd profiles show odoo19-* warns you when the profile uses a lower version.

Enterprise: any *-ee profile expects an ./enterprise directory with the Odoo Enterprise add-ons (subscription required) next to addons/ before you run rkd up -d.

docs.title: Container Management
docs.text:
• Deploy Odoo (start containers in detached mode):
rkd up -d
  • Check the status of your containers:
rkd status
  • Stop all containers:
rkd stop
  • Restart the containers:
rkd restart
  • Remove containers:
rkd down
  • Remove containers and their associated volumes:
rkd down -v
  • Force environment rebuild:
rkd build
  • Build and restart containers in one step:
rkd build --rebuild
  • View container logs:
rkd logs
  • Follow logs in real-time for a specific container:
rkd logs <container_name> -f

docs.title: Environment Sharing
docs.text:
• Package your entire environment to share with other developers:
rkd pack                   # full environment + database backup + filestore
rkd pack --no-db           # environment files only
rkd pack -o /tmp/my.zip    # choose the output path
rkd pack --db-name demo    # pick the database, when the project has several
rkd pack --yes             # no prompt: continue without a backup if the DB container is down
  • Unpackage a shared .zip project into your directory:
rkd unpack                 # full setup: ports, SSH, database restore
rkd unpack --build         # rebuild the Docker image first (recommended on a first run)
rkd unpack --no-restore    # skip the database restore
rkd unpack --ssh-key NAME  # use this key from ~/.ssh/ instead of asking
rkd unpack --no-ssh        # the project has no private repositories
rkd unpack --yes           # accept the suggested fixes for port conflicts

docs.title: What never enters the ZIP
docs.text:
Since 3.9.2. rkd pack used to hand the sender's own credentials to whoever received the file.

The archive leaves out .ssh/, .rkd/secrets/, .rkd/instance.yaml, .rkd/deploy.yaml, traefik/certs/acme.json and every *.env (except *.env.example), and no symbolic link enters it — a link pointing at a secrets file used to carry that file out of the project. Hard links are caught by inode. It also drops .rkd/deploy_backups, which holds the sender's own backup history and is of no use to anybody else. The closing panel names everything that was left out, which is exactly the list the receiver has to rewrite on their side.

Two credentials do travel, on purpose. odoo_pg_pass and config/odoo.conf are packed, because without them the shared environment does not start: Compose mounts the first as a Docker secret and the Dockerfile copies the second at build time. They are the local credentials of the environment being handed over, which is the point of the ZIP — so treat a Rocketdoo archive as something you send to a teammate, not something you publish.

Since 3.10 the verifier reads the first 64 KiB of each entry looking for PEM headers instead of trusting filenames, and separates the two cases: a red warning when a file Rocketdoo declares secret slipped in, and a calmer amber one when something merely reads like a private key — an Enterprise project typically carries about five of those, from Odoo's own localizations.

The ZIP also no longer packs itself, nor the backups left by previous packs (3.8.1).

docs.title: A restored copy gets its own Compose identity
docs.text:
Since 3.9. When the Compose project name in the archive is already used by another directory on your host, rkd unpack renames the copy instead of colliding with the original.

Two copies sharing one project name meant Compose treated the original's containers as belonging to the copy — recreating and destroying them — and the restore ran DROP DATABASE against the original's data. The rename is all-or-nothing and covers name:, image:, every container_name (including the commented Mailpit one), volume definitions and references, and db_host in config/odoo.conf.

Detection asks docker compose ls and looks at volume labels, because a project brought down with rkd down (no -v) is absent from the first while its volumes are still on disk. If Docker does not answer, nothing is renamed: Rocketdoo never guesses. The CLI asks — Rename this copy to <suggested>? — --yes accepts, and the GUI accepts automatically.

The copy also takes its own ports when the original holds them, and the message distinguishes "this port is in use" from "this port belongs to the other copy, which is switched off".

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
• Delete .Identifier files generated by WSL2 when copying files from Windows:
rkd del -i
  • Preview which files would be deleted (dry run, no files removed):
rkd del -i --dry-run
  • Bulk update module packages loaded as public repositories using Gitman: (This command must be executed inside the container.)
gitman update

docs.title: One command that is not in --help
docs.text:
New in 3.10. The epilogue of rkd --help ends with a line about a rocket still on the pad. It is a hint.

rkd launch

A rocket climbs a field of stars on the terminal's alternate screen — like vim or less, so your scrollback is left alone — and the flight ends on one of six lines of the "Zen of Odoo" about customizing with Studio. The six lines are in Spanish, whatever your locale. The animation is skipped without a TTY, with TERM set to dumb or unknown, or on a terminal smaller than 25×13, but the message is printed anyway, so rkd launch | cat still reads. It respects NO_COLOR.

docs.title: ⚙️ Continuous Integration (rkd ci)
docs.text:
New in 3.5. rkd ci writes a GitHub Actions workflow for your project — not for Rocketdoo. It lints your addons and, optionally, installs them against a real Odoo.

  • Generate .github/workflows/rkd-ci.yml:
rkd ci init

On a terminal this asks you when the install job should run, defaulting to pull_request. Answer up front, or skip the question entirely:

rkd ci init -y                              # take the default, no question
rkd ci init --install-trigger never         # lint only

Option Description --install-trigger When the install job runs: pull_request, push, manual, never. Asked interactively if omitted; pull_request without a terminal --force Overwrite a workflow that differs from the current render -y, --yes Skip the install-trigger question and take the default

It never overwrites a file that differs from what it would write, without --force, whether the difference came from you editing it by hand or from a config change. What it tells you: Created: for a new file, already up to date when it matches, a warning naming --force when it differs, and Overwritten: when you pass it.

  • Regenerate the files a clean clone does not carry:
rkd ci prepare

config/odoo.conf and odoo_pg_pass are gitignored — they hold credentials — so a fresh clone does not have them. The build copies config/odoo.conf into the image (COPY ./config/odoo.conf) and compose feeds odoo_pg_pass in as a secret at startup, so without this step a clean checkout gets nowhere. It also syncs the addons_path. It never overwrites an odoo.conf that already exists, which is what the output above is reporting.

Pass --admin-passwd to set the master password it writes; otherwise one is generated.

  • List the installable modules Odoo can actually reach:
rkd ci modules

Prints them comma-separated on stdout, for MODULES=$(rkd ci modules) inside the workflow.

docs.title: What the generated workflow does
docs.text:
Job When it runs What it costs Lint Every pull request, pushes to the default branch, and manually Seconds Install Pull requests against the default branch, by default Several minutes

The workflow triggers on pull_request, on push to the default branch only, and on workflow_dispatch. Pushing a feature branch with no pull request open runs nothing. The lint job runs ruff check over addons/ and then rkd deploy validate -p addons.

The install job is the expensive one, which is why it is limited by default. On private repos the Free plan gives 2,000 Actions minutes a month shared across your whole account; public repos do not consume that quota. Change the trigger with --install-trigger if that split does not suit you.

Those numbers are GitHub's, not Rocketdoo's, and GitHub changes them: check the current Actions billing.

Manifest linting. Ruff's default rules flag B018 on every __manifest__.py — by Odoo's own definition it is a bare dict literal — so the generated workflow passes --extend-per-file-ignores "**/__manifest__.py:B018". Without it the lint job is red on every Odoo project.

rkd ci init signs off with "the lint job runs ruff with its default rules". The generated workflow does add the exception above — the message is the thing that is imprecise, not the workflow.

docs.title: What is outside the generated path
docs.text:
• Enterprise, and private repos over SSH. The workflow is still written, without the install job and with the reason as a comment: a runner has no access to your private sources.
  • Private Gitman sources. rkd ci init warns if gitman.yaml has git@/ssh:// sources, but it cannot tell a private HTTPS repo from a public one — that build fails on the runner with no warning up front.
  • Deploying to staging. Deliberately left out for now: rkd deploy has no headless way to generate a deploy.yaml, so the generated workflow only lints and installs.

docs.title: 📧 Mail — Mailpit Email Testing (rkd mail)
docs.text:
Mailpit is a local SMTP server and web UI that captures all outgoing emails from Odoo instead of actually sending them. Ideal for testing email workflows without affecting real users.

  • Enable Mailpit (start service + configure Odoo SMTP automatically):
rkd mail on
  • Disable Mailpit and restore default SMTP settings:
rkd mail off
  • Check the current Mailpit status:
rkd mail status

  • Open the Mailpit web interface in the browser:
rkd mail open

docs.title: Mailpit picks a free host port
docs.text:
Since 3.9.1. The host ports are no longer fixed at 1025 and 8025, so two Rocketdoo projects with Mailpit enabled no longer collide.

rkd mail on reads the ports declared in the compose file, keeps them when they are free, and takes the next free one when they are not — counting ports declared by a sibling project that is currently switched off, not only ports in use right now. It prints which ones it took and writes them into the compose file as it enables Mailpit; rkd mail off only comments the block out and leaves those numbers in place, so the project keeps the same ports next time and a browser bookmark keeps working.

rkd mail open and rkd mail status read the real published port rather than assuming 8025, which is why the status panel is the place to look for the web UI address.

The internal port never changes. Inside the Docker network Odoo always talks to mailpit:1025; only the host side moves.

docs.title: The mail server record in Odoo
docs.text:
New in 3.3. On top of the compose and odoo.conf toggle, on/off/status now read and write an ir.mail_server record in your database, named Mailpit (rkd), with smtp_host = mailpit and sequence = 1. Before this, enabling Mailpit configured the transport but left Odoo still pointing at whatever mail server the database had.

off only archives the record (active = false) — it never deletes, so a mail server of your own is never at risk. The record is matched by name plus smtp_host: if you rename it by hand, off will not find it (and says so) and on will create a new one.

Multi-database projects need --db:

rkd mail on --db my_database
rkd mail status --db my_database
rkd mail off --db my_database

With exactly one database in the project it is picked automatically. With two or more and no --db, the command neither reads nor writes the record, and tells you.

The db container has to be up for this part. If it is not, the compose and odoo.conf toggle still happens and the mail server step is reported as not done — run rkd up -d and retry the same command.

Known limit. sequence = 1 does not guarantee Mailpit wins. Odoo filters mail servers by from_filter before ordering by sequence, so another active server whose from_filter matches the sender can beat Mailpit anyway. rkd mail status warns when other active servers exist, but it does not read or write from_filter.

docs.title: 🌐 Traefik Reverse Proxy (rkd traefik)
docs.text:
Traefik allows you to expose your local Odoo instance using a custom domain, both for local development (HTTP) and production environments (HTTPS with Let's Encrypt).

  • Enable Traefik for this project (interactive wizard — prompts for domain and mode):
rkd traefik on
  • Enable with specific options:
rkd traefik on --domain myproject.local --mode local
rkd traefik on --domain myproject.com --mode production --email ops@example.com

--email was added in 3.11. With --domain, --mode, --traefik-dir and --email the wizard runs unattended, which is what a script or a CI job needs.

  • Disable Traefik for this project (restores direct port access):
rkd traefik off
  • Show Traefik integration status:
rkd traefik status
  • Show step-by-step guide to configure local domains (/etc/hosts and WSL2):
rkd traefik guide

Traefik modes: - local — HTTP only, custom domain via /etc/hosts. - production — HTTPS with automatic Let's Encrypt certificate.

off only removes the override. Your docker-compose.yaml is never touched, so reconfiguring means rkd traefik off and then on again. When .rkd/instance.yaml exists, rkd traefik status also points at rkd instance traefik, which is the remote counterpart of this command.

This command configures the proxy on your machine. To install Traefik on the server an environment deploys to, see Installing Traefik on the VPS.

docs.title: 🚀 VPS Instance Deployment (rkd instance)
docs.text:
The instance command deploys a complete Odoo instance to a VPS. It supports two deployment types:

  • docker — transfers Dockerfile + compose files and builds on the VPS.
  • native — installs Odoo via official apt packages on the server.

Since 3.13, the choice is about packaging, not about what you get. Both paths install the Gitman repositories in the same place and build the same canonical addons_path — enterprise, extra-addons, nested directories, gitman. Until 3.13 the native path put Enterprise last and ignored nested directories.

  • Configure stage/production environments interactively (saves to .rkd/instance.yaml):
rkd instance init

The wizard adds, it no longer replaces (3.11). Each environment is offered separately — Reconfigure stage?, Configure a prod environment? — and whatever you do not touch is kept exactly as it was. Reconfiguring stage used to delete prod. The deployment type is asked once and applies to new environments; an existing one keeps its own. A summary at the end reports each environment as added, kept, updated or removed.

  • Start over, dropping whatever you do not configure again:
rkd instance init --force

docs.title: What the wizard asks
docs.text:
Per environment: deployment type, VPS host, SSH port and user, authentication (an SSH key chosen from ~/.ssh/, or the name of an environment variable holding a password), Odoo version, and — for Docker — image tag, domain, Let's Encrypt email, PostgreSQL version, database user and name. Then the master password, the source database (see below), whether to use Enterprise and how it should reach the server, whether to use Gitman, the PostgreSQL resource profile (small for a VPS under 2 GB RAM, medium for 4–8 GB, large for 16+), Odoo's own performance settings (see below) and the remote path.

Enterprise reaches the server two ways (3.11). rsync transfers your local enterprise/ directory; clone fetches odoo/enterprise on the VPS through a forwarded SSH agent, so no credential is left on the server. Before 3.11 choosing Enterprise declared the directory in the Dockerfile, the compose file and both addons_path entries — and put it nowhere, so Odoo started without the add-ons.

Rocketdoo refuses to write here if this is not a Rocketdoo project (no Dockerfile and docker-compose.yaml side by side), because the wizard stores credentials under .rkd/.

docs.title: Seeding an environment with a local database
docs.text:
New in 3.14. By default a deployed environment starts from a fresh database. The wizard also offers Restore local database '<name>' (with its filestore) for each database it finds, and the deploy then dumps it, transfers it, restores it on the server and neutralizes it.

It happens once per environment: the deploy writes a rkd.seeded_from mark inside the restored database and a redeploy never restores again. To seed a second time you have to drop the database on the VPS by hand — deliberately so, because the alternative is a flag that overwrites a client's production with a development dump. A database the target already serves and Rocketdoo did not seed is never overwritten: the deploy refuses and says so.

Neutralization differs by target. Both regenerate the database UUID, disable the Mailpit mail server — which points at a host that does not exist on the VPS, so leaving it would make every outgoing mail fail silently — and repoint web.base.url at the environment's domain, dropping web.base.url.freeze so the new value is the one Odoo uses. Staging only also disables scheduled actions, mail servers and payment providers; doing that to production would stop the crons of the instance you are launching.

The admin password of a seeded database is not replaced — its users keep theirs — and the closing panel says so instead of promising a new one.

docs.title: Tuning Odoo per environment
docs.text:
New in 3.15. The performance block of the deployed odoo.conf — workers, cron threads, memory and time limits — is configurable per environment instead of being fixed by the environment's name.

The wizard asks one question, defaulting to no:

Performance: 2 workers, 1024 MiB soft limit, 120s request limit.
Tune Odoo's performance settings for this server? [y/n] (n)

Saying yes walks through the seven values with the effective ones as defaults, so answering through changes nothing. They are stored under resources in that environment's entry of .rkd/instance.yaml:

environments:
  prod:
    resources:
      workers: 4
      max_cron_threads: 2
      limit_memory_soft: 2147483648    # bytes, per worker
      limit_memory_hard: 2684354560    # bytes, per worker
      limit_time_cpu: 600              # seconds
      limit_time_real: 1200            # seconds
      limit_request: 8192

Every field is optional, and an absent one keeps the default the environment name implies, which is what Rocketdoo emitted before this existed — so an instance.yaml without a resources block deploys exactly as it used to.

stage prod workers 1 2 max_cron_threads 1 1 limit_memory_soft 768 MiB 1 GiB limit_memory_hard 1 GiB 1.5 GiB limit_time_cpu 60 s 60 s limit_time_real 120 s 120 s limit_request 8192 8192

The case this exists for: a project whose odoo.conf raises limit_time_cpu and limit_time_real to 600/1200 for large imports and heavy reports. Deploying it used to write 60/120 over those values, cutting both operations in half — and editing the file on the server was no fix, because the next deploy rewrites it, on both paths and with no guard, so a hand-tuned value is silently lost.

Two mistakes are refused rather than deployed: a negative number, and a limit_memory_hard below limit_memory_soft — Odoo kills the worker instead of recycling it.

Memory limits are per worker, not per server. Rocketdoo's memory pre-flight check adds up workers + max_cron_threads + 2 processes at the soft limit, plus PostgreSQL's share, and since 3.15 it uses this environment's effective values rather than Rocketdoo's own constants — so a resources block that does not fit the VPS blocks the deploy before anything is written, naming the figures. Its hint now points at workers and limit_memory_soft, which is the knob that exists.

Not in the GUI. The Instances screen has no performance fields: configure them with rkd instance init or by editing .rkd/instance.yaml. Since 3.15 saving an environment from the GUI carries an existing resources block over instead of wiping it.

Sizing is not read from the server, on purpose. Physical RAM is not available RAM — a VPS may be running PostgreSQL and something else beside it — so Rocketdoo does not guess a number for you; it checks the one you chose against what it measured.

resources and the PostgreSQL resource profile are different knobs. small/medium/large sizes PostgreSQL (shared buffers and connections); resources tunes Odoo.

One behaviour change for native deploys (3.15). The Docker template pinned limit_request = 8192 while the native odoo.conf declared none of the three time limits and fell back to Odoo's own defaults. Both paths now write the same answer, so an existing native environment moves from limit_request 65536 to 8192 — the worker recycles more often, which is the more conservative of the two. The other two limits do not move.

docs.title: The pre-flight, and a dry run that writes nothing
docs.text:
Since 3.11. Both deployers open with a pre-flight: a single read-only SSH session that collects facts about the server and sorts them into blockers and warnings. A blocker stops the deploy before anything is written.

The checks: vps connection, docker, sudo, remote path, disk space, memory, ssh key file, ssh agent, ssh agent socket, gitman file, gitman repositories, gitman dependency script, enterprise directory, enterprise repository, postgresql version, database identifiers, native host, seed database, traefik and public url. Seeding adds two blockers of its own — the source database must still exist, and a dump from a PostgreSQL newer than the server's will not restore — and raises the disk space floor by twice the size being seeded.

--dry-run used to print "Deployment successful" without touching the VPS, while still writing a secrets file locally. It now runs that same pre-flight, connects only to read, writes nothing, and exits non-zero when something blocks — so this chain finally means what it looks like:

rkd instance deploy --env prod --dry-run && rkd instance deploy --env prod
  • Deploy to the staging environment:
rkd instance deploy --env stage
  • Deploy to production (with confirmation prompt):
rkd instance deploy --env prod
  • Deploy to production skipping the confirmation:
rkd instance deploy --env prod --yes
  • Run the pre-flight without deploying (dry run):
rkd instance deploy --env prod --dry-run

Confirmations. Deploy <env> to <host>? defaults to no, prod adds a warning, and an environment configured to be seeded asks again — on prod you have to type prod literally.

  • Show status of all configured deployment targets:
rkd instance status

docs.title: Installing Traefik on the VPS
docs.text:
New in 3.12. The Odoo container only exposes its port. Something has to answer on 80 and 443 and obtain the certificate, and that is Traefik.

rkd instance traefik --env prod
rkd instance traefik --env stage --traefik-dir /opt/traefik --email ops@example.com

It installs Traefik on that environment's server — once per host — with the same configuration rkd traefik renders locally, reading host, user and the Let's Encrypt address from .rkd/instance.yaml. Running it again is safe: files you tuned and certificates already issued are kept, and an installation of your own is respected and reported rather than replaced. It exits with an error when ports 80/443 are held by something else, or when nothing ends up serving that Odoo.

Native environments are refused: they have no reverse proxy in front today.

The deploy never runs it for you. Ports 80 and 443 belong to the host, not to one project, so installing a proxy there is a decision you make once, explicitly.

The closing panel no longer claims a URL it did not test (3.12). After deploying, Rocketdoo probes the domain from the VPS over HTTP and HTTPS and distinguishes four outcomes: Odoo answers, Traefik answers but cannot reach Odoo, the certificate was not issued, or nothing answers. When nothing answers it names rkd instance traefik --env <env> as the fix. A native deploy promises http://<host>:8069 and says plainly that there is no reverse proxy yet.

docs.title: 🖥️ Graphical User Interface (rkd gui)
docs.text:
Launch the Rocketdoo web GUI in your browser. Provides full container management, live logs, mail, deploy, and more — all without typing commands.

  • Start the GUI on the default port (8070):
rkd gui

Since 3.4, read the URL it prints. Every run generates a session token and the GUI does not load without it: http://127.0.0.1:8070/?token=<token>. Restarting rkd gui issues a new one. See Graphical Interface (GUI).

Since 3.8, reaching it without the token is not a dead end. http://localhost:8070 on its own — which is where the VSCode port notification sends you — now shows a card with a field to paste the token into, and the browser tab remembers the last one that worked.

Since 3.8, an occupied port fails honestly. rkd gui used to print the full panel with a freshly minted token and the bind error underneath; copying that newer URL got you a 401, because only the server that is actually listening knows its own token. It now checks the bind before printing anything, explains that the URL which works is the one the other session printed, offers a free port, and exits with an error.

  • Start the GUI on a custom port:
rkd gui --port 9090
  • Start the GUI and open the browser automatically:
rkd gui --open
  • Start the GUI for a project in a specific directory:
rkd gui --cwd /path/to/project

The GUI is available at http://localhost:8070 by default — on the tokenised URL it prints. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

Learn more about the GUI

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
In this section, we highlight some of the most frequent errors encountered when using the development environment.

We also encourage users of this framework to report any incidents or bugs not covered here via our Help Desk, so we can update and review each case accordingly.

  • First and foremost: since v3, ROCKETDOO is not a repository template at all. You install it as a package — pipx install rocketdoo — and run rkd scaffold inside an empty directory. Cloning or forking the Rocketdoo repository is only for contributing to Rocketdoo itself.

docs.title: Failed to Install requirements.txt
docs.text:
When faced with this error, the system suggests using Python virtual environments, which is an excellent approach. However, if you prefer to install the requirements on your PC without a virtual environment, you can resolve it with the following command:

pip3 install -r requirements.txt --break-system-packages

If you want to use a virtual environment, execute:

python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Failure to Install ROCKETDOO
docs.text:
Similar issues may occur during the framework installation:

Solution:

pip3 install rocketdoo --break-system-packages

docs.title: Launching ROCKETDOO from the Wrong Directory
docs.text:
It is common to attempt launching ROCKETDOO from the project's root directory; for example, as shown in the image, launching from the root of your created repository (my-dev-on-odoo) when it should actually be run inside the rocketdoo subfolder:

my-dev-on-odoo/rocketdoo

To resolve this, press CTRL + C to cancel the current action, then navigate to the correct directory and launch again:

cd rocketdoo
rocketdoo

If done correctly, you should see the ROCKETDOO welcome screen as below:

For further assistance, please submit a ticket to our Help Desk

docs.title: Debugging in Odoo
docs.text:
One of the main steps to debug code in Odoo is to enter the container. Inside the container, you will be able to use the code debugging tool; in addition to having access to all the core modules of the system, both for the Community and Enterprise editions.

To access our container and be able to navigate inside the Odoo system, we must verify that our container is running. For this, we can use a terminal on our PC, a terminal inside VSCode, or use the recommended extension "Dev Container".

docs.title: Container Running
docs.text:
Once we have our container running, we need to press the following key combination:

SHIFT + CTRL + P

And in the search palette, we need to search for the following:

Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container

This will allow us to connect remotely to the container where our Odoo instance is running. It is important, once inside the container, to wait for VSCode to finish indexing our entire workspace.

Once indexing is 100% complete, we will be able to access our Debugging tool (recommended extension) and execute any of our debugging options; whether it's the Python debugger, the JavaScript debugger, or both:

"Odoo: Debug-Breakpoints"

"Debug POS JavaScript in Chrome"

"Odoo Full Debug (Python + JS)"

Once our debugger is running, we can start using breakpoints and reviewing our developments quickly and safely.

docs.title: Demo Video: How to Debug Odoo with VS Code?
Deployments
docs.text:
This new functionality in RKD allows us, either during or after completing and locally testing our developments, to deploy the corresponding module to an Odoo environment. This can include Odoo SH, a VPS, or Dockerized Odoo instances.

To perform this action, our framework now provides a set of new commands to simplify the configuration of deployment targets. These commands allow the developed modules to be tested in a development or staging environment by functional consultants or QA testers.

It is no longer sufficient to test our modules only in a local environment and validate their correct behavior. We can now move this validation process closer to a production-like instance and, at the same time, ensure that the module is permanently deployed within the client’s system.

In this section of the documentation, we will list these new commands and explain how to use them according to each use case.

Two different commands, two different jobs. rkd deploy — this page — ships modules to an Odoo that already exists, whether that is Odoo.sh or a server of your own. rkd instance does the other half: it installs the whole Odoo instance on a VPS, from the Docker image or the native packages up to the database and the reverse proxy. If there is nothing running on the server yet, you want rkd instance first.

docs.title: Before Getting Started:
docs.text:
It is important to note that in our development environment, the directory intended for the modules we develop is addons/

Therefore, the Odoo developer must always create or clone the module they want to work with inside this directory, since the framework will search for modules in this location by default.

docs.title: Deployment Commands:
docs.text:
rkd deploy --help
  • Help command for deploy
rkd deploy init
  • Command to start the deployment configuration process
rkd deploy list-modules
  • Command to list the modules prepared for deployment
rkd deploy config
  • Command to fully verify the deployment targets defined
rkd deploy run
  • Command to execute the deployment
rkd deploy run --target
  • Allows specifying the configured target for deployment
rkd deploy run --target <test> --module <my_module>
  • This command allows you to explicitly specify which module you want to deploy
rkd deploy validate
  • Validates the modules before deployment

rkd deploy run --dry-run never contacts the target. It scans addons/, lists the modules and refuses a --module that does not exist, and then prints Dry-run completed successfully without talking to the server at all. Treat it as a placeholder rather than a rehearsal — rkd deploy validate is what actually inspects your modules. The dry run of rkd instance deploy is a different thing entirely: it runs the full pre-flight against the server and reports real blockers.

On a password target, the dry run still asks for the password and stores it. The deployer is built before the dry-run branch is reached, so a target configured with password authentication prompts VPS Password: and writes .rkd/secrets/vps_<target>.env (mode 600) — a dry run that leaves a credential on disk. Use key authentication, or export the password variable, if that matters to you.

Fixed in 3.14.3, if you deploy from the GUI. The Deploy and Validate Modules buttons failed on every call — the first through a method that did not exist, hidden behind a wide except that reported success anyway, the second showing an empty Validation errors card for every project. Both now go through the same entry point as the CLI. On 3.14.2 and earlier, deploy from the terminal.

docs.title: Deployment to Odoo SH
docs.text:
To get started, the developer must have developer access to the Odoo SH environment and repository permissions in order to execute a deployment on an Odoo SH instance. For this reason, when creating the development environment, it is also essential to select the option to manage private repositories, as this will list the SSH keys connected to the developer’s GitHub repository.

For this and all deployment scenarios, we will use the following command:

rkd deploy init

This command initializes the deployment configuration by guiding us step by step through the required parameters to later execute the application deployment.

Let’s review the steps one by one:

  • First, it informs us that a deployment configuration already exists and asks whether we want to overwrite it.
  • Then, it asks whether we want to auto-detect the module(s) to deploy. If there is more than one module in the addons/ directory, it is recommended to select "n" (No) and later specify the module using the --module option.
  • Next, it asks for the directory where the module is located. By default, it suggests addons, so we enter addons.
  • We indicate that we want to create a deployment target.
  • We then select the environment where the deployment will be performed. In this case, we select Odoo SH.

    • This section is critically important, as the requested parameters correspond to the deployment target itself.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
• In the Odoo SH configuration, the system first asks for the project ID. This can be obtained by checking the project in the dashboard, either from its URL or its name. The URL usually follows this structure: odoo.sh/project/project-id where project-id is the project ID.

  • Next, it asks for the deployment branch and suggests development or staging by default. It is important to know the name of the branch created under Staging (in this example, it is "test"). If a branch name that does not exist in the project states is provided, Odoo SH will create the branch during deployment under the Development state, as is standard behavior.

  • In the next step, it asks whether we will connect to the environment via API. If the developer has an existing token, this option can be used; otherwise, selecting NO will use the repository permissions instead.

  • The Git remote name is almost always origin, which is why this option is suggested by default (RECOMMENDED).

  • Finally, at this stage, it is necessary to copy and paste or enter the repository URL where the application will be deployed.

  • After creating and naming the target, the system confirms that it has been added and asks whether we want to create another target.

docs.title: Backup Configuration
docs.text: • The system offers the option to create backups of our deployments.

docs.title: Module Validations
docs.text:
• In this section, the system requests validation of the module structure.
  • Finally, it indicates that the deployment configuration has been successfully created.

This configuration can also be reviewed using the rkd deploy config command, which lists all the created targets.

docs.title: Running a Deployment on Odoo SH
docs.text:
rkd deploy run --help
